case_content.title: Prompt #1 - Magazine Distribution
case_content.content: A magazine publisher is trying to decide how many magazines she should deliver to each individual distribution outlet in order to maximize profits. She has massive amounts of historical data for sales volumes through these outlets and a well constructed internal accounting system. How should she go about computing an appropriate number?

case_content.title: Interviewer Guidance - Initial Approach
case_content.content:
Possible solution:

The best way to tackle this one, without going into a huge Economic Order Quantity quantitative analysis, is not so much to start asking questions as to set out and outline analysis and fill in as you go.

case_content.title: Interviewer Guidance - Framework
case_content.content:
The candidate should apply basic microeconomics and statistics. To maximize profits, marginal revenues should be set equal to marginal costs.

The marginal revenue for a magazine would be its cover price times the probability that it will be sold. The probability of sale, with an appropriate confidence interval, could be established in some manner from the historical data. The marginal costs could be obtained from the internal accounting data.

case_content.title: Expected Analysis - Fact Gathering
case_content.content:
The analysis should determine the optimal delivery quantity for each individual outlet by comparing marginal revenue and marginal cost.

For each additional magazine delivered to an outlet, estimate:

1. The marginal revenue: cover price multiplied by the probability that the additional magazine will be sold.
2. The marginal cost: the incremental cost of printing, shipping, handling, stocking, and any unsold magazine cost or return cost.

Historical sales data should be used to estimate the probability that an incremental copy will be sold at each outlet. The estimate should include an appropriate confidence interval to account for demand variability. Internal accounting data should be used to estimate the relevant marginal cost for each additional copy.

The publisher should continue adding magazines to a given outlet until the expected marginal revenue of the next magazine no longer exceeds its marginal cost.

case_content.title: Data / Calculations
case_content.content:
Available data:
- Massive amounts of historical sales-volume data by distribution outlet
- Well constructed internal accounting system

Core calculation:
- Profit is maximized where marginal revenue = marginal cost
- Marginal revenue per additional magazine = cover price x probability that the magazine will be sold
- Probability of sale should be estimated from historical data, with an appropriate confidence interval
- Marginal cost should be obtained from internal accounting data

Decision rule:
- Deliver an additional magazine to an outlet if expected marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost
- Stop adding magazines when expected marginal revenue is equal to or less than marginal cost

case_content.title: Key Findings
case_content.content:
The optimal number of magazines for each outlet should be determined using marginal analysis rather than a simple average of historical sales. Because the publisher has strong historical sales data and accounting data, she can estimate both the probability of selling each incremental copy and the marginal cost of supplying it.

The key insight is that the marginal revenue of the last delivered copy declines as more copies are delivered because the probability of sale falls. The publisher should supply copies up to the point where the expected revenue from the next copy equals its marginal cost.

case_content.title: Final Recommendation
case_content.content: Based on your analysis, what recommendation would you give the client?

case_content.title: Interviewer Guidance - Final Recommendation
case_content.content:
A strong candidate should recommend computing outlet-level delivery quantities by equating marginal revenue and marginal cost. The marginal revenue of each additional magazine equals the cover price multiplied by the probability that the copy will be sold, estimated from historical sales data with an appropriate confidence interval. The marginal cost should be drawn from the internal accounting system.

The publisher should deliver magazines to each outlet until the expected marginal revenue of the next copy no longer exceeds its marginal cost. A detailed discussion of basic microeconomics and statistics may be necessary.
